text:
Can you help me write the project summary for a grant application? I'm the managing attorney at a two-lawyer legal aid clinic that represents tenants facing eviction. We're applying to our state bar foundation for $90,000 to hire a third attorney for two years.

Facts:
- Last year 1,140 eviction cases were filed in our county. We represented the tenant in 163 of them.
- In the cases where we represented the tenant, 58% ended with the tenant staying in the home or getting at least 60 days to move. We don't have a comparable number for tenants without a lawyer.
- We turned away about 300 tenants last year because no attorney was free.
- Our two attorneys each carry about 80 open cases. One of them is leaving in June.
- A third attorney would cost $78,000 a year with benefits. The foundation's maximum award is $45,000 a year.
- The county gives us $60,000 a year, and that contract is up for renewal in October.

The project summary has to be 300 words or less.

I can help. A few questions first, because the answers change what the summary can safely claim:

1. **How will you cover the other $33,000 a year?** The attorney costs $78,000 and the foundation's maximum is $45,000. Reviewers will spot that right away. Do you have the rest committed or pending (county money, another grant, reserves)? If none of it is secured yet, should I say that plainly?

2. **Is the attorney leaving in June being replaced separately?** If not, a "third attorney" would really keep you at two, and the foundation might see the request as backfilling a vacancy rather than adding capacity. Is there a replacement plan, and when exactly does the new hire start?

3. **What can you commit to in numbers?** For example, how many more tenants per year a third attorney would represent (roughly 80 open cases at once, but how many closed per year?), and whether you'd track outcomes the same way. A specific target will help the application more than anything else.

4. **How solid is the county contract?** Has the county said anything about renewing the $60,000 in October, good or bad? It's a risk the foundation may already know about, so I'd rather address it than leave it out.

5. **Who reads this, and what do they already know about you?** Have you had foundation funding before, and if so, what did you report? Do you have any outside support, like a judge, the court clerk, or a partner agency who sends you referrals?

6. **Is there anything else the reviewers might already know or will find out?** For example, a weak number, a past grant that fell short, or turnover. And what's the clinic's name and the submission deadline?

If you don't know some of these, that's fine. I'll write around them without guessing.

1. A family fund has pledged $20,000 a year for two years toward the new attorney. The rest of the gap comes from our general budget.

2. I don't have a separate replacement plan to point to. The attorney who's leaving in June has agreed to spend her last month training the new hire. I don't have an exact start date.

3. I don't have a number for how many more tenants a third attorney would close per year. I can commit to reporting to the foundation every six months on cases opened and how they ended. I can also ask the county clerk for court-wide outcome data starting in January, so we'd have a comparison next year.

4. I can't promise the county will renew the $60,000 in October.

5. I don't know.

6. We have no figure for what happens to tenants without a lawyer in our county. Our last attorney opening took 5 months to fill. The clinic is the Tenant Defense Project, and I'm Maria Chen, managing attorney. The application is due March 3, and the foundation decides in May.

I wrote it as keeping you at two attorneys, not adding a third. With the June departure and no plan to replace her, the new hire brings you back to two. If the summary says "third attorney," reviewers will see the June departure in the same paragraph, and that would hurt you more than describing the grant accurately. The accurate version still makes a strong case: without this grant, the number of tenants you can represent drops by about half.

<final_document>
**Tenant Defense Project: Keeping Eviction Defense Available in [County]**

Last year, 1,140 eviction cases were filed in [County]. The Tenant Defense Project, a two-attorney legal aid clinic, represented the tenant in 163 of them. In 58% of those cases, the tenant stayed in the home or got at least 60 days to move. We turned away about 300 more tenants because no attorney was free.

Our capacity is about to fall by half. Each of our attorneys carries about 80 open cases, and one leaves in June. Our last attorney search took five months, so we need to begin recruiting as soon as funding is certain.

We request $90,000 over two years ($45,000 per year) toward a staff attorney position that costs $78,000 a year with benefits. A family fund has pledged $20,000 a year for both years. The clinic will cover the remaining $13,000 a year from its general budget. With this grant, we can hire promptly and keep two full-time eviction defense attorneys rather than one.

We will measure results the same way we do now. Every six months, we will report to the Foundation the number of cases opened and how each one ended. Starting in January, we will request court-wide eviction outcome data from the [County] Clerk. We currently have no figure for how tenants without a lawyer fare. With that data, by the end of the first grant year we can compare outcomes for represented and unrepresented tenants and report the difference to the Foundation.

Even at full strength, two attorneys cannot meet the need: last year we turned away 300 tenants. Without this grant, the number of tenants we can represent will fall by half.
</final_document>

It's about 280 words. Some notes before you submit:

- **"Third attorney":** If you actually plan to replace the departing attorney some other way, tell me and I'll change the summary back. Don't call it a third attorney unless that's true.
- **The training month probably won't work.** The foundation decides in May, she leaves in June, and your last search took five months. That's why I left the training overlap out of the summary. If you mention it elsewhere, either start recruiting before the decision or describe a different handover, like written case files and a transition memo.
- **County contract:** I left it out because 300 words isn't enough room to explain it well. Reviewers will likely ask about it, though. Address it in the budget or sustainability section, including what happens to your $13,000 share if the county doesn't renew.
- **The 58%:** The summary presents it only as your own result and doesn't compare it to anything, since you have no comparison number. The clerk data plan covers that gap.
- Fill in **[County]**, and check whether the foundation wants your name and title on the summary page.
